items.mnemonic: Under the ROOF a CHILD kneels at a low desk, copying the same shape over and over until the ink runs dry: a CHARACTER.
A PERSON lifts ONE BAMBOO slip to their MOUTH, reads the question aloud, then brushes the ANSWER on the back.
A LID of cloud closes over the town; a PERSON hurries home as EVENING deepens, and one last STROKE of light slides down the sky: NIGHT.
Strike a bronze temple bell and the SOUND rolls out in widening rings; this kanji is that SOUND, standing alone with nothing else in the picture.
The KING lifts a jug of WATER, lets one DROP fall into the cup, then tilts it until a steady stream follows: he knows how to POUR.
A traveler hangs up the SWORD, takes down the BROOM, pulls the COVER off the bedding and shakes out the CLOTH: home at last, a true RETURN.
A singer hammers a NAIL into the stage post to hang her lantern, opens her MOUTH as wide as a YAWN, and out pours a SONG that fills the hall.
Across all of ASIA the storyteller searched and found one HEART that had turned sour and cold; everyone who met it agreed it was BAD.
Inside a square ENCLOSURE a surveyor paints a CROSS to mark the well and adds a DROP for the spring; the sketch becomes a DIAGRAM.
Walk the same ROAD past the FRAME of the gate, the plot of EARTH and the MOUTH of the well seven mornings in a row, and you have walked one WEEK.
You ARRIVE under the ROOF, slide the door shut behind you, and the quiet space that closes around you is your ROOM.
STOP, take a SMALL step, STOP again, then add one more STROKE of the foot in the dust: the slow, steady rhythm of a WALK.
The WIND bellies out a sail and sends paper kites spinning over the rooftops; this kanji is the WIND itself, a gust curled around a swirl of dust.
The CLAN beats fibers of THREAD flat in a wooden vat, lifts the mat and peels off a thin white sheet: PAPER.
Soot from the kitchen fire settles on the window night after night until the whole pane is BLACK; this kanji is that BLACK, a smoked-over village above the flames.
THREE friends, each a PERSON stretching after the long winter, stand under the warm SUN as the first buds open: SPRING.
A paper lantern glows RED over the earth with fire licking beneath it; this kanji is that RED, the color of the lantern, the ember and the setting sun.
A young plant stands over a well of clear water and the whole picture is BLUE; this kanji is that BLUE, fresh and cool, the color of sky and new leaves.
Where travelers come to EAT, under one wide ROOF, a HEAP of folded futons waits in the corridor: the BUILDING that welcomes guests.
The old owner lies flat on the bench like a CORPSE, napping, until customers ARRIVE; he sits up, dusts the counter, and the SHOP is open.
A bolt of silk is BOUND UP tight, then unwound in a long COIL across the floor, every turn dyed a different shade: COLOR.
Dirt flies up behind a sprinter's heel as the body leans forward; this kanji is the RUN itself, a figure with legs stretched long.
The GRAIN is cut and stacked, and the stubble is set on FIRE so smoke drifts over the reddening hills: AUTUMN.
ONE hot afternoon, sweat drips from your NOSE while your WALKING LEGS drag along the shimmering road: SUMMER.
A chick beats its FEATHERS again and again above the WHITE nest, failing, trying once more, until one morning it flies: to LEARN.
A flock of SHEEP stands on the shore gazing at WATER with no far bank at all: the OCEAN.
A PERSON picks a DIRECTION, bundles spare CLOTHES on a stick over one shoulder and sets off down the road: TRAVEL.
By the light of the MOON a tailor presses a wax SEAL onto a folded robe and hands it over with the RIGHT HAND: new CLOTHES.
A thin crescent moon with a single star caught inside it hangs over the fields as the light fades: EVENING.
A PERSON asks the neighbor for TWENTY coins and swears to bring them back before the SUN goes down: to BORROW.
Each morning the SUN rises, a SMALL BIRD shakes out its FEATHERS and sings a different tune, one for every WEEKDAY.
Two ribs hang inside a butcher's wooden frame, marbled and fresh: MEAT. The kanji is that cut of MEAT, the frame with the ribs inside.
A PERSON drives a STAKE into the ground, ties a bag of SHELL money to it and tells a friend to take what is needed: to LEND.
A SMALL lamp burns under the FRAME of the roof; the wide MOUTH of a doorway opens onto a floor of packed EARTH: the great HALL.
A BIRD perched on a branch, its eye a single dot and four tail feathers trailing below: the kanji is the BIRD itself.
Time to EAT: at the foot of the CLIFF the cook scoops steaming rice with the RIGHT HAND into bowls for the climbers: a MEAL.
BOUND UP in blankets, a student mutters with their MOUTH, kicks their LEGS awake and summons every bit of POWER to finish the page: EFFORT.
WALKING LEGS stop at a river sealed with ICE; two frozen drops hang below the heel: WINTER.
Hold a RULER up to the SUN and its shadow shrinks to ONE short line directly beneath it: DAYTIME, high noon.
Among the GRASS a PERSON leans against a TREE, pours hot water over dried leaves and breathes in the steam: TEA.
A boy with HORNS of tied-up hair swings a BOW too big for him and scratches one proud STROKE in the dirt where the arrow landed: the YOUNGER BROTHER.
A COW seen head-on: two horns, a long face and a tail swishing below. The kanji is the COW itself.
A FISH with a pointed head, a scaled body and a tail of four quick flicks: the kanji is the FISH itself, drawn swimming upward.
A big MOUTH on long LEGS: the one who speaks first and walks ahead of the little ones, the OLDER BROTHER.
A big creature with one floppy ear drawn as a drop at its shoulder: a DOG. The kanji is the DOG itself, sitting up and begging.
A WOMAN NOT YET grown, still in a short kimono and chasing butterflies through the garden: the YOUNGER SISTER.
A WOMAN pulls on a hat shaped like a LID, ties a CLOTH apron and heads to market to run the household errands: the OLDER SISTER.
Where the river WATER bends, TWENTY villages open the MOUTH of their gates to a HUSBAND coming home from the ancient empire of CHINA.
A STONE lies at the foot of a cliff, round and heavy and cool to the touch; the kanji is that STONE under the overhang.
Grains burst from a single stalk in every direction: RICE. The kanji is that stalk of RICE, a cross with four flying grains.
A head with hair standing up and one eye wide, balanced on a NECK; the kanji is the NECK and head together, seen from the front.
A SAMURAI calls across the courtyard so loudly that even a CORPSE would sit up to listen: a VOICE.
A BEAN balanced on top of a HEAD, wobbling with every step; the kanji is the HEAD itself with the little dish perched on top.
A RAY bursts from a lamp carried high on two legs, and the whole dark room turns bright: LIGHT.
A HORSE with a flowing mane and four legs drawn as flames beneath the body: the kanji is the HORSE at full gallop.
A KING stands between heaven and earth, joining them with one upright line; the kanji is the KING himself.
STAND at the CLIFF edge while the wind pulls STREAKS of hair across your HEAD; what the wind uncovers is your FACE.
A PERSON sews THREAD of many colors into the shape of a CLOUD on silk, stitch by stitch, until it becomes a PICTURE.
A YOUTH bends a BAMBOO stalk and lets it spring back to tickle a friend's nose, and both collapse in a LAUGH.
Down the ROAD in no fixed DIRECTION a PERSON and a CHILD chase a runaway kite: to PLAY.
GRASS grows under the SUN until it stands TEN hands high across the whole meadow: GRASS.
WATER, rice and patience rest together in the SAKE JAR until the smell turns sweet and sharp: ALCOHOL.
Under the ROOF a BED is swept clean with a BROOM, a COVER is pulled over it, and a RIGHT HAND tucks you in: SLEEP.

examples.en: to sleep, to go to bed

items.mnemonic: A row of rice-grain teeth inside an open jaw, with a stop sign above telling you to brush: TOOTH. The kanji is the TOOTH itself, drawn in the mouth.
RAIN that falls so soft and dry you sweep it off the doorstep with a BROOM: SNOW.
A COW stands on its LEGS in the shallows while the farmer pours bucket after bucket of WATER over its back: to WASH.
WATER stretching to ETERNITY in every direction, and you pull yourself through it stroke by stroke: to SWIM.
A BIRD opens its MOUTH at first light and the whole valley wakes to the CHIRP.
From MOON to SUN a PERSON on tired WALKING LEGS wanders from stall to stall, tasting everything, until the BELLY is round and full.
Weave BAMBOO over a TREE frame and leave one small hole for the EYE to peek inside: a BOX.
The SUN is BOUND UP in clouds on the horizon, a MOUTH yawns and tired LEGS stretch toward the futon: EVENING.
Under the ROOF the WELL has frozen solid; ONE child counts EIGHT icicles of ICE hanging from the eaves: COLD.
A HEART so overrun with errands that by nightfall it lies as still as the DECEASED: BUSY.
The DOG hunts out in the open, but this creature crouches in the GRASS at the edge of the RICE FIELD, waiting for a mouse: a CAT.
Already BIG, and then one extra DROP of weight is added underneath: FAT.
A BOAT with a TABLE bolted to the deck and the round MOUTH of a porthole in the side: a SHIP.
GRASS, WHITE bark, two HORNS of dried root and sap from a TREE are ground together in a bowl: MEDICINE.
Inside the ENCLOSURE the EARTH is raked, the MOUTH of a little pond is dug, and CLOTHES dry on a line among the flowers: a GARDEN.
Under the LEAN-TO a PORTER sets down his load and steps out to STRETCH his back in the open GARDEN.
A CURVE of bent reed woven through a basket frame; the kanji is the CURVE itself.
A BROOM in one hand, one brisk STROKE of the brush in the other and a MOUTH that gives orders: the young master everyone addresses as YOU.
GRASS brushes a NET of eyelashes, a COVER settles over the mind, and EVENING carries you off into a DREAM.
On the ROAD a trail of spilled RICE grains leads off in three directions at once, and you are LOST.
The ROAD crosses bare EARTH, passes the MOUTH of a valley and wears out your CLOTHES before it ends: FAR.
A HOLE in the wall, PRIVATE and small, where the HEART sits and watches the rain: a WINDOW.
TWENTY times the SUN has climbed and fallen since those days, and twenty more: LONG AGO.
Before the ALTAR you bend low like a FISHHOOK and hold the bow a moment before rising: COURTESY.
Hollow out a TREE knot and carve a NEGATIVE sign on the side so nobody dares leave it empty: a CUP.
COMPARE every face around the table in the WHITE lantern light and count: ALL of them are here.
One EYE closes, then another, until the whole POPULACE of the village has shut theirs: SLEEP.
A memory lies DECEASED somewhere inside the HEART, and no one can find where it was buried: FORGET.
A TREE grows inside a tight ENCLOSURE with nowhere to spread its branches: TROUBLE.

examples.en: to be troubled, to be at a loss

items.mnemonic: The SUN goes down and only SOUND is left to guide you along the path: DARK.
The SUN breaks through and the sky turns BLUE from one edge to the other: the weather will CLEAR UP.
A HAND slides a PRIVATE handful of coins across the counter without a word: to PAY.
Back along the ROAD beneath the CLIFF, a RIGHT HAND holds out the umbrella you lent last week: GIVE BACK.

examples.en: to return something, to give back

items.mnemonic: A PERSON gets ONE letter before the SUN sets because the runner took the CROSS path through the fields: CONVENIENCE.
A RIDE on the back of a tall tree, with branches for a seat and the horizon for a road; the kanji is the RIDE itself.
Once a year the guard will STOP, lean the HALBERD by the door and cut one SMALL notch in the post to count how many YEARS OLD the house is.
A single leaf of a DOOR hanging from its hinge with the lintel across the top; the kanji is the DOOR itself.
